title: Bipartisan Bill or Executive Action? Congress Passes Historic Housing Legislation While Trump Pushes Deregulation
subtitle: Senate passes bipartisan housing bill 89-10 to ban Wall Street investors while Trump signs executive orders eliminating environmental regulations for home construction

conservative.headline: Trump Cuts Red Tape to Build More Homes While Senate Passes Bloated Housing Bill Full of Washington Spending
conservative.byline: As seen on Fox News, Daily Wire, White House
paragraphs: President Trump is finally taking action to fix America's housing crisis by eliminating the burdensome regulations and green mandates that drove up home costs under Biden, even as the Senate passes a mixed-bag housing bill that includes some good ideas but leaves key House reforms on the cutting room floor.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner didn't mince words about who's to blame for the housing affordability crisis. As Fox News reported, Turner said homeownership is the bedrock of the American Dream, but that foundation crumbled under the Biden administration as red tape made building homes and securing mortgages increasingly more expensive.

The White House laid out the problem in stark terms in its fact sheet on Trump's executive orders. According to the administration, layers of red tape, slow permitting processes, and costly environmental mandates imposed by progressive policymakers at the state, local, and federal level have made it harder and more expensive to build homes in America. Trump's executive orders directly target these barriers by streamlining environmental reviews, eliminating unnecessary wetlands permitting delays, and curtailing expensive green building codes that add tens of thousands of dollars to home prices.

Home builders are celebrating Trump's decisive action. NAHB Chairman Bill Owens praised the president for taking bold actions to empower home builders to build the housing supply America needs. The construction industry has been hamstrung for years by environmental regulations that serve progressive ideological goals rather than helping working families afford homes.

Meanwhile, the Senate passed its housing bill 89-10, which includes some Trump-backed provisions like banning Wall Street from buying up single-family homes. But House conservatives are raising red flags about what got left out. Rep. Mike Flood warned that the Senate removed important bipartisan House provisions that would have slashed barriers to building more homes, suggesting the bill still contains too much Washington spending and not enough real reform.

Several principled conservatives including Senators Thom Tillis, Ted Cruz, Rand Paul, and Mike Lee voted against the bill because it represents government intrusion into the free market by telling investors what they can and cannot buy. While banning Wall Street from buying homes sounds good politically, these senators understand that heavy-handed government mandates often have unintended consequences that hurt the very people they're supposed to help.

Trump's executive action strategy shows he's serious about cutting costs for American families immediately, not waiting for Congress to craft another massive spending bill dressed up as housing reform. By eliminating Biden's regulatory burden, Trump is putting the American Dream of homeownership back within reach for millions of families.

liberal.headline: Senate Passes Landmark Housing Bill to Ban Wall Street Investors, But Trump Dismisses It and Pushes Environmental Rollbacks
liberal.byline: As seen on NBC News, NPR, PBS NewsHour
paragraphs: The Senate just passed historic bipartisan legislation to stop Wall Street from buying up American homes and squeezing families out of homeownership, but President Trump is dismissing the housing crisis entirely while pushing dangerous environmental rollbacks that will harm communities of color the most.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who co-sponsored the groundbreaking legislation with Republican Tim Scott, made the stakes crystal clear. As NBC News reported, Warren declared that homes are for the families who live there, not for Wall Street investors who figured out another way to make a buck. The bill would ban large institutional investors owning 350 or more homes from purchasing additional single-family properties, directly targeting the financial speculation that has driven housing costs through the roof.

Warren didn't hold back in identifying the culprits. Speaking to NPR, she condemned corporate landlords that are squeezing families out of homeownership. This bill represents exactly the kind of bold action needed to protect working families from Wall Street greed, yet Trump is more interested in gutting environmental protections than signing legislation that actually helps people afford homes.

In fact, Trump has made his priorities shamefully clear. At a House Republican retreat, Trump said that the people are demanding the SAVE America Act voter suppression bill, not housing legislation, adding dismissively that they don't talk about housing, they don't talk about anything. This stunning admission reveals that Trump sees housing affordability as a political inconvenience rather than a crisis affecting millions of American families.

Instead of supporting bipartisan solutions, Trump is using executive orders to roll back critical environmental protections under the guise of housing affordability. Matthew Tejada of the Natural Resources Defense Council warned PBS NewsHour that overburdened communities, which are typically communities of color, Indigenous communities and low-income communities, will again suffer most from these actions. Trump is gutting Clean Water Act protections, eliminating energy efficiency standards, and removing environmental review requirements that protect vulnerable communities from pollution and flooding.

The contrast could not be more stark. Senate Democrats and Republicans came together to pass meaningful legislation with an overwhelming 89-10 vote, showing that solving the housing crisis doesn't have to be partisan. Yet Trump is more focused on appeasing fossil fuel companies and construction industry donors by eliminating the safeguards that protect public health and the environment.

When Congress actually does its job and passes bipartisan legislation to help families, Trump dismisses it and pushes deregulation that will poison communities and make climate change worse. This isn't about housing affordability—it's about prioritizing corporate profits over people and using the housing crisis as an excuse to destroy decades of environmental progress.

factcheck.headline: Separating Fact from Spin
paragraphs: Both sides are presenting selective versions of the same events to fit their narratives. Conservatives emphasize Trump's deregulation while downplaying the bipartisan Senate bill. Liberals highlight the landmark legislation while portraying all deregulation as dangerous. Here is what actually happened.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ The Senate vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act passed the Senate 89-10 on March 12, 2026, with support from both parties. Co-sponsors were Republican Tim Scott and Democrat Elizabeth Warren.

✓ The bill targets Wall Street investors: The legislation bans large institutional investors that own 350 or more single-family homes from purchasing additional properties. It also requires build-to-rent operators to sell homes to occupants after seven years.

✓ Trump signed multiple executive orders: On March 13-14, 2026, Trump signed executive orders titled "Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home Construction" and "Promoting Access to Mortgage Credit." These orders direct EPA and Army Corps of Engineers to review Clean Water Act wetlands permitting and call for eliminating green building codes and energy efficiency requirements.

✓ Trump's conflicting positions: Trump publicly urged Congress to ban Wall Street from buying homes during his State of the Union address, signed an executive order in January doing exactly that, but then told House Republicans he won't sign any legislation until the SAVE America Act (voter ID bill) passes first.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: Biden-era regulations are solely responsible for housing unaffordability. Reality: Housing costs have been rising for decades due to multiple factors including zoning restrictions, land availability, labor shortages, material costs, and yes, some regulatory burdens. Attributing the entire crisis to Biden-era environmental rules oversimplifies a complex problem that predates the last administration.

⚠️ Claim: The Senate bill is a "bloated" spending package. Reality: The bill actually focuses primarily on regulatory reforms and market restrictions rather than massive new spending programs. It streamlines environmental reviews for housing construction while also restricting investor purchases. House conservatives oppose it largely because they want stronger provisions, not because it spends too much.

✓ Fair Point: Regulatory delays do add costs. Conservatives are correct that permitting processes, environmental reviews, and building code requirements can add time and expense to housing construction. The question is whether the protections these regulations provide justify those costs, not whether the costs exist at all.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: Trump is "dismissing" the housing crisis. Reality: Trump signed multiple executive orders specifically focused on housing affordability and previously called for banning Wall Street investors. His statement that he won't sign bills until the SAVE Act passes is a negotiating tactic, not proof he doesn't care about housing. Whether his priorities are correct is debatable, but he hasn't ignored the issue entirely.

⚠️ Claim: All environmental deregulation will harm communities of color. Reality: Some environmental regulations disproportionately affect low-income communities by making housing construction more expensive in those areas. The environmental justice argument cuts both ways—regulations can protect vulnerable communities from pollution, but they can also price those same communities out of housing. The impact depends on which specific regulations are changed and how.

✓ Fair Point: Wall Street investors have driven up housing costs. Liberals are correct that institutional investors purchasing single-family homes in bulk have contributed to housing unaffordability by competing with individual buyers and converting ownership opportunities into permanent rentals. This is a real problem worthy of legislative action.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

Both approaches address real problems but neither is a complete solution. The Senate bill tackles investor speculation but won't by itself create more housing supply. Trump's deregulation might speed construction but won't stop Wall Street from buying what gets built. As Senator Scott noted, it's not a Republican issue or a Democrat issue—it's an issue about helping families afford homes.

The real test will be whether the House passes any version of the Senate bill, whether Trump actually signs it despite his SAVE Act ultimatum, and whether his executive orders survive legal challenges. The fate of the legislation remains uncertain with House conservatives demanding changes and Trump's shifting priorities.

The Bottom Line: America faces a genuine housing affordability crisis that requires both increased supply and restrictions on speculative investment. The Senate passed bipartisan legislation addressing both, while Trump is pursuing deregulation through executive action. Whether either approach significantly improves affordability for working families remains to be seen, but the political gamesmanship from both sides isn't helping families who can't afford homes today.
